answers.text:
"Superposition" here is a specific technical term from mechanistic interpretability research — the study of how neural networks encode information — rather than an everyday word. It refers to a network cramming more distinct features into its neurons than it has neurons to spare, by letting neurons respond to multiple, unrelated things at once instead of each neuron standing for one clean concept.

The article spells this out later using the "dense" code example: a representation is in superposition when it "can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons (just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers)." The price of this efficiency is that "Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons" — but "It isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets." Recovering the individual features packed together this way needs a nonlinearity, not just a straight linear read-off, since "if there's no composition, one can instead store exp(m) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them."

As you may know, the term comes from Anthropic's earlier paper "Toy Models of Superposition," which this note is explicitly building on and referencing — the article later notes that paper "might be seen as fundamentally exploring this trade-off, although it casts things in terms of an equivalent idea of feature sparsity rather than composition." This note's whole project is to separate that idea of superposition from a second, competing idea — "composition" — that people often lump together under the same label of "distributed representations."

answers.asked: An informal note on the relationship between superposition and distributed representations by Chris Olah.
answers.text:
Chris Olah is a machine learning researcher best known for his work on interpretability — trying to understand what's actually happening inside neural networks rather than treating them as black boxes. He was a founding member of Anthropic's interpretability team and, before that, worked on similar problems at OpenAI and Google Brain, where he was involved in early, influential visual explanations of how neural networks "see" (feature visualization, and the interactive-essay style associated with the journal Distill, which he co-founded).Chris Olah is a Canadian machine learning researcher and a co-founder of Anthropic, known for his work on neural network interpretability, particularly mechanistic interpretability, and for research and tools that visualise internal representations in neural networks. Before Anthropic, he worked on interpretability research at Google Brain, OpenAI, and Anthropic, starting as an intern at Google Brain in 2015 and working his way up to a research scientist. In 2017 he co-founded the interactive machine learning publication Distill, and a paper published there led to a job at OpenAI, where in 2018 he left Google Brain to lead OpenAI's interpretability team. In 2020 he left OpenAI and co-founded Anthropic a year later.

This background matters for the piece you're reading: Olah's whole career has centered on "reverse engineering" neural networks to figure out what's actually happening inside them, which is exactly the motivation stated early in this note — the idea that decomposing a network's internal representations is necessary to really understand what it's doing. The note itself is a step in that broader interpretability project, distinguishing two things ("composition" and "superposition") that get lumped together under the older neuroscience/AI term "distributed representations."

answers.asked: What does "superposition" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "superposition" is the strategy of packing more features into a layer than it has neurons, by letting each neuron take part in many different features rather than dedicating one neuron to one thing. The clearest illustration is the "dense" code: there's another kind of distributed representation that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons (just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers). Such codes are sometimes called "dense". In our framing, it's maximal superposition. The trade-off is spelled out right after: Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons. But note that there are also lots of costs to this. It isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets.

The article defines superposition against a second idea, "composition" — building objects out of independent, separately-meaningful feature-neurons (like a "green" neuron and a "square" neuron combining) [spya-qcd003 spya-xcdtte]. The core argument of the piece is that these two are not just points on one "distributed vs. local" spectrum, but genuinely different, competing strategies for using up a fixed budget of representational capacity: If one has \(m\) bits to encode stimuli, we can think of there as being \(\exp(m)\) volume. Storing \(n\) features which arbitrarily compose together requires \(\exp(n)\) volume; so we can only store fully composable features in \(m\) bits. But if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them. That is, composition and superposition are two different ways to allocate the exponential volume.

Why this matters to the argument: the article's stake is interpretability — whether you can look at a network's representation and read off, with simple linear operations, what features are present. Composition preserves that: Compositional representations are also extremely favorable from an interpretability perspective – we can understand them in terms of individual components, despite the potentially exponential space of composition. Superposition breaks it, since features overlap on the same neurons and can't be cleanly separated by a linear probe. The opening of the piece frames this as the whole motivation: We care a lot about superposition and the structure of distributed representations because decomposing representations into independent components is necessary to escape the curse of dimensionality and understand neural networks. And the conclusion returns to exactly this point: Understanding the structure of representations is important because they're fundamentally at the heart of efforts to reverse engineer and mechanistically understand neural networks. When neural network representations are distributed in the sense we call "composition", it is possible to understand them in terms of a linear number of independent features rather than an exponential amount of volume. This seems critical if we hope to truly understand neural networks.

So the concept of superposition matters here less as a curiosity of neuroscience-derived toy examples, and more as the reason interpretability is hard: it's the strategy networks likely use to be efficient, and it's precisely the strategy that resists the linear-probe methods researchers want to use to understand them, as flagged early on with the local-code example: In our toy example, it would be very reasonable to probe for the existence of a feature like "red", and in the above example, a linear probe would certainly be able to predict it! However, despite this, it doesn't seem like the above example should be understood as having a "red" feature.

In this context, monosemantic means "having one meaning": each neuron responds to exactly one thing and nothing else. The passage is describing Thorpe's "local code," where there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, so a single neuron fires only for, say, a red circle — never for anything else, and no other neuron overlaps with it in meaning.

This term sets up a contrast that runs through the rest of the piece. A monosemantic neuron is the opposite of a polysemantic one, which fires in response to several unrelated features (as happens under superposition, discussed later when the "dense" and "semi-distributed" codes are introduced). Olah's broader interpretability work treats monosemanticity as desirable because a neuron with one clean meaning is easy to interpret directly, whereas polysemantic neurons — the product of packing more features into a network than it has neurons for — need to be decomposed before they can be understood. So flagging the local code as "monosemantic and without superposition" here is doing double duty: it names the property and quietly foreshadows why superposition (its opposite number in this note) makes interpretation harder.

answers.asked: In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition.
answers.text:
This is defining a term the article is going to use throughout: "monosemantic" describes a neuron that stands for exactly one thing — here, one specific (shape, color) pair, like "red circle" — rather than a neuron that fires for several unrelated things at once. Its opposite, "polysemantic," would be a neuron that responds to multiple unrelated features, which is what happens under superposition.

The second half of the sentence is doing the real conceptual work: it's tying "monosemantic" directly to the absence of superposition. Superposition, in the framework this note is building on, is the strategy of cramming more features into a network than it has neurons for, by letting neurons each represent several things and relying on sparsity (and a nonlinearity) to sort them back out later — this is explained a few sentences later in the piece, where storing more items than you have "bits" requires giving up the one-neuron-one-meaning property. The "local code" being described here is the opposite extreme: there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, so nothing is compressed and nothing is shared or overlapping — hence no superposition, and each neuron's meaning is clean and singular, hence "monosemantic."

Worth knowing if you haven't encountered it elsewhere: "monosemantic" is a term Olah and colleagues at Anthropic use across their interpretability work (notably in the earlier "Toy Models of Superposition" paper this note builds on) specifically to talk about whether a neuron's activation can be given one clear interpretation — it's contrasted with "polysemantic neurons," which respond to several unrelated features and are much harder to interpret. This passage is the first time in the piece that the local code (one neuron per shape-color pair) gets mapped onto that vocabulary, setting up the later contrast with the "semi-local," "semi-distributed," and "dense" codes, which all introduce superposition in different degrees.

answers.text:
In this piece, "monosemantic" describes the pure "local code" example: a setup where there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, so each neuron has exactly one meaning — it fires for one specific combination and nothing else "We'll start with what Thorpe calls a pure "local code". In this setup, there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair. In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition." [spya-kcjqdw]

It matters to the argument because it's the reference point against which everything else in the piece is defined. A monosemantic neuron is, by definition, the opposite of superposition — where instead a single neuron would represent several unrelated features. The local code example uses monosemantic neurons and needs one per combination, which the article contrasts later with the "semi-local"/compositional code (fewer neurons, built from independent color and shape features) and the "dense" code, which uses superposition to pack many combinations into very few neurons this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition... there's another kind of distributed representation that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons... Such codes are sometimes called "dense". In our framing, it's maximal superposition. The later "semi-distributed" code is described as polysemantic rather than monosemantic — units that respond to a few features rather than just one — which is exactly the shift from monosemanticity that superposition introduces Although these units begin to have some meaning – they're polysemantic, but only respond to a few features – it seems more natural from our perspective to think of this code from the perspective of linear combinations of neurons (ie. directions) as corresponding to features. [spya-vw7xv6]

My inference is that starting with the monosemantic local code lets the article isolate the two strategies (composition and superposition) cleanly: the local code has neither, so adding composition or superposition to it separately shows what each strategy buys and costs, before the piece turns to how they can be mixed [spya-kcjqdw spya-xcrca8 spya-vefv29].
